description: Standardized human-readable record per obligation, keyed by obligation_id. Every record carries summary, impacts, implications (to the beverage industry), topics, the governing CFR or national equivalent, an action, and source backlinks. This is the normalized basis for the tiered briefing and the exportable records database. Authored for internal research; confirm against primary text before any compliance or marketing use.

us-fed-gras-overhaul.summary: GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) lets a substance be added to food without FDA premarket approval if qualified experts agree it is safe; for decades a company could self-affirm GRAS and never tell FDA. FDA has signaled it will close that self-affirmation path and is re-reviewing older additives.
us-fed-gras-overhaul.impacts: Any ingredient a beverage relies on under self-affirmed GRAS may need a notification or removal; preservatives such as BHA and BHT are early re-review targets.
us-fed-gras-overhaul.implications: A beverage maker can no longer assume a self-affirmed ingredient is settled; the industry must hold audit-ready safety files for every additive in use.
us-fed-gras-overhaul.action: Inventory every self-affirmed GRAS ingredient in the portfolio and assemble its safety file now; flag any on FDA's re-review list for a reformulation contingency.

backlinks.label: FDA: How U.S. FDA's GRAS Notification Program Works

us-fed-dye-phaseout.summary: Certified color additives are the synthetic FD&C dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3) listed and batch-certified by FDA. In 2025 FDA and HHS announced a push to phase out petroleum-based dyes, and FDA had already revoked the authorization for FD&C Red No. 3 in food in January 2025.
us-fed-dye-phaseout.impacts: Flavored and colored sparkling drinks using certified dyes face reformulation to exempt-from-certification colors; Red No. 3 is a hard removal item.
us-fed-dye-phaseout.implications: A color change is also a claims event for the industry: it can support or undercut a 'no artificial colors' statement, so color sourcing becomes a marketing decision, not just an R&D one.
us-fed-dye-phaseout.action: Map every SKU's color source; for any certified dye, plan a Part 73 alternative and coordinate the label and claims change.

us-fed-upf-definition.summary: There is no legal definition of 'ultra-processed food' yet; FDA and USDA announced they are jointly developing one. Once it exists it becomes a lever for warnings, school restrictions, and marketing pressure.
us-fed-upf-definition.impacts: Sweetened and heavily formulated beverages, especially those using non-nutritive sweeteners, are likely to land inside whatever definition emerges.
us-fed-upf-definition.implications: The industry faces a medium-term repositioning question; a definition could reshape claims, school access, and consumer perception across the category.
us-fed-upf-definition.action: Track the joint FDA and USDA definition work and pressure-test the portfolio against the leading candidate definitions.

us-fed-fop-labeling.summary: FDA proposed a front-of-package nutrition label (a 'Nutrition Info' box) rating Saturated Fat, Sodium, and Added Sugars as Low, Medium, or High on the front panel, amending 21 CFR Part 101.
us-fed-fop-labeling.impacts: For a sweetened drink, added sugar is the most likely 'High' trigger and would reshape the front panel; a zero-sugar line is comparatively well positioned.
us-fed-fop-labeling.implications: Front-of-package ratings could shift category-wide purchasing toward lower-sugar options and make added sugar a visible point-of-sale signal.
us-fed-fop-labeling.action: Model each SKU against the proposed thresholds and sequence any front-panel redesign to absorb the box in one change.

us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.summary: FDA's updated 'healthy' claim rule (21 CFR 101.65) requires a food to fit a food-group model, not just hit nutrient thresholds. It was effective in 2025 with a compliance date of February 25, 2028.
us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.impacts: Any beverage that carries or implies 'healthy' must be re-checked against the new definition before the compliance date; adding vitamins to an unhealthy base no longer qualifies.
us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.implications: The industry loses a long-used marketing lever and must substantiate wellness positioning against a stricter federal standard.
us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.action: Audit every product that uses or implies 'healthy' and remove or substantiate the claim before 2028.

backlinks.label: FDA: Use of the Term Healthy on Food Labeling

us-fed-caffeine-guidance.summary: Caffeine added to cola-type beverages is GRAS up to 0.02 percent under 21 CFR 182.1180. FDA is working on voluntary caffeine-labeling guidance for the energy and functional categories and has warned about concentrated caffeine.
us-fed-caffeine-guidance.impacts: A caffeinated line must keep added caffeine within the GRAS basis for its category and be ready for voluntary labeling expectations.
us-fed-caffeine-guidance.implications: Energy and functional positioning carries added labeling and safety scrutiny, and intersects Canada's stricter supplemented-foods regime.
us-fed-caffeine-guidance.action: Confirm per-serving caffeine against the GRAS basis and prepare cautionary-statement copy for markets that expect it.

backlinks.label: FDA: Spilling the Beans on Caffeine

us-ca-ab418.summary: California AB 418, the California Food Safety Act, bans the manufacture or sale in California of foods containing brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben, or FD&C Red No. 3, effective January 1, 2027. It parallels FDA's federal revocations of BVO (2024) and Red No. 3 (2025).
us-ca-ab418.impacts: Any California-sold formula containing BVO or Red No. 3 must be reformulated before January 1, 2027; given the federal revocations these are national removal items.
us-ca-ab418.implications: California sets the template other states copy, so its bans effectively become the national floor for the industry.
us-ca-ab418.action: Confirm with R&D and suppliers that no California-sold formula contains the four banned substances and treat BVO and Red No. 3 as national removals.

cfr.citation: Federal parallel: BVO authorization revoked (former 21 CFR 180.30)
Federal parallel: FD&C Red No. 3 (21 CFR Part 74)

us-ca-prop65.summary: Proposition 65 is California's 1986 right-to-know law: it requires a warning when a product exposes a person to one of roughly 1,000 listed chemicals above a safe-harbor level. For beverages the drivers are trace heavy metals and acrylamide.
us-ca-prop65.impacts: Trace heavy metals carried in by botanicals, colors, concentrates, or water can trigger a warning obligation or a bounty-driven lawsuit; bottled water and botanical drinks carry the most exposure.
us-ca-prop65.implications: Exposure, not harm, triggers enforcement, so the industry carries ongoing testing and supplier-indemnity cost regardless of actual risk.
us-ca-prop65.action: Maintain annual heavy-metal and acrylamide testing for California-sold products, secure supplier attestation and indemnity, and warn where a safe-harbor level cannot be met.

ca-fed-supplemented-foods.summary: Health Canada's Supplemented Foods Regulations govern foods with added supplemental ingredients (including caffeine and certain vitamins), requiring a Supplemented Food Facts table, cautionary statements, and caffeine limits.
ca-fed-supplemented-foods.impacts: A caffeinated or functional beverage sold in Canada may need cautionary statements and must stay within Canadian caffeine limits, which can differ from the US basis.
ca-fed-supplemented-foods.implications: Canada is a stricter functional-beverage market, so US formulations and labels may not port directly across the border.
ca-fed-supplemented-foods.action: Map any Canada-distributed SKU to the supplemented-foods requirements: caffeine limit, cautionary statements, and the Supplemented Food Facts table.

mx-fed-nom051.summary: Mexico's NOM-051 front-of-pack labeling requires black octagon warning seals for products high in calories, sugars, saturated fat, or sodium, plus disclaimer legends when a product contains non-nutritive sweeteners or added caffeine.
mx-fed-nom051.impacts: A sweetened or non-nutritive-sweetened beverage sold in Mexico likely carries one or more octagon seals and a sweetener disclaimer, and faces marketing-to-children restrictions.
mx-fed-nom051.implications: Mexico is the strictest front-of-pack regime the portfolio meets and a preview of where warning-label policy can go.
mx-fed-nom051.action: For Mexico-distributed SKUs, determine the octagon seals and sweetener or caffeine legends triggered and confirm packaging compliance.

us-ca-ab660.summary: California AB 660 standardizes date labels: a date, if used, must use the 'BEST if Used By' or 'USE by' family of terms, with 'sell by' banned, effective July 1, 2026.
us-ca-ab660.impacts: Packaging copy on California-sold products must conform by July 1, 2026; this is a label-copy change, not a formula change.
us-ca-ab660.implications: Date-label standardization is spreading and reduces the flexibility brands have in package wording.
us-ca-ab660.action: Update date-label copy for California SKUs before July 1, 2026.

us-ca-ab2316.summary: California AB 2316 bans six synthetic dyes from foods sold through school channels, effective December 31, 2027.
us-ca-ab2316.impacts: Only products that reach the school channel are affected; core retail lines are not directly covered.
us-ca-ab2316.implications: School channels are becoming a distinct, stricter market that the industry must formulate for separately.
us-ca-ab2316.action: Confirm whether any SKU reaches school channels and review its colors.

us-ca-ab1264.summary: California AB 1264 is an enacted school-focused ultra-processed-food law; CDPH must define terms by June 1, 2028, and the definition names non-nutritive sweeteners such as sucralose.
us-ca-ab1264.impacts: Sucralose-sweetened drinks in the school channel may be restricted once the definition is set.
us-ca-ab1264.implications: California's UPF definition will likely become a reference other states and channels adopt.
us-ca-ab1264.action: Track the CDPH definition and assess school-channel exposure for non-nutritive-sweetened SKUs.

us-ca-ab2244.summary: California AB 2244, introduced February 2026, proposes a voluntary 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal with retailer good-faith identification, using a UPF definition tied to prior California law.
us-ca-ab2244.impacts: Certification could be a shelf differentiator at large retailers; non-certified products may face a perception gap.
us-ca-ab2244.implications: A voluntary seal can still pressure the whole category to reformulate to qualify.
us-ca-ab2244.action: Decide whether to pursue certification if the bill advances.

us-ca-state-gras.summary: A California bill would create a state-level GRAS review process, part of the broader state GRAS-reporting trend.
us-ca-state-gras.impacts: Adds a state reporting and review burden on additives used in California-sold products.
us-ca-state-gras.implications: A state-by-state GRAS patchwork would multiply compliance cost across the industry.
us-ca-state-gras.action: Monitor the bill and inventory self-affirmed GRAS additives in use.

us-ia-school-food.summary: Iowa enacted a school-food ingredient law naming synthetic dyes and other additives.
us-ia-school-food.impacts: Affects products sold through Iowa school channels only.
us-ia-school-food.implications: Part of the multistate school-food wave that fragments the school market.
us-ia-school-food.action: Confirm school-channel exposure and the colors used.

us-ne-school-food.summary: Nebraska enacted a school-food ingredient law naming synthetic dyes and other additives.
us-ne-school-food.impacts: Affects products sold through Nebraska school channels only.
us-ne-school-food.implications: Part of the multistate school-food wave that fragments the school market.
us-ne-school-food.action: Confirm school-channel exposure and the colors used.

us-tn-school-food.summary: Tennessee enacted a school-food ingredient law naming synthetic dyes and other additives.
us-tn-school-food.impacts: Affects products sold through Tennessee school channels only.
us-tn-school-food.implications: Part of the multistate school-food wave that fragments the school market.
us-tn-school-food.action: Confirm school-channel exposure and the colors used.

us-nj-state-gras.summary: New Jersey is debating a state GRAS reporting bill.
us-nj-state-gras.impacts: Potential state reporting burden on additives used in New Jersey-sold products.
us-nj-state-gras.implications: Adds to the state GRAS-reporting trend and the cost of a patchwork.
us-nj-state-gras.action: Monitor the bill and inventory self-affirmed GRAS additives.

us-ny-state-gras.summary: New York is debating a state GRAS reporting bill.
us-ny-state-gras.impacts: Potential state reporting burden on additives used in New York-sold products.
us-ny-state-gras.implications: Adds to the state GRAS-reporting trend and the cost of a patchwork.
us-ny-state-gras.action: Monitor the bill and inventory self-affirmed GRAS additives.

us-nj-ingredient-bill.summary: New Jersey filed one of the first state ingredient bills in 2023.
us-nj-ingredient-bill.impacts: Could restrict named additives in New Jersey-sold products if advanced.
us-nj-ingredient-bill.implications: An early signal that the ingredient patchwork reaches beyond California.
us-nj-ingredient-bill.action: Confirm the bill's current status against state text.

us-wv-ingredient-ban.summary: West Virginia enacted a statewide ingredient ban, subject to litigation.
us-wv-ingredient-ban.impacts: Could block sale of affected SKUs in West Virginia once effective.
us-wv-ingredient-ban.implications: States can ban outright, so the strictest state effectively sets the national floor.
us-wv-ingredient-ban.action: Confirm effective dates and the affected ingredients against state text.

us-tx-label-warning.summary: Texas label-warning legislation has been slowed by litigation but keeps recurring.
us-tx-label-warning.impacts: Could require warning text on labels of Texas-sold products if enacted.
us-tx-label-warning.implications: Signals that label-warning policy is spreading beyond California.
us-tx-label-warning.action: Monitor the litigation and any refiling.

us-multistate-ingredient-patchwork.summary: More than 140 ingredient bills across 42 states (13 enacted) target over 100 ingredients, with California setting the template.
us-multistate-ingredient-patchwork.impacts: A nationally distributed product generally must meet the strictest state's rule or maintain separate formulations.
us-multistate-ingredient-patchwork.implications: The patchwork is the central cost driver, pushing the industry toward function-tagged ingredient management and proactive reformulation.
us-multistate-ingredient-patchwork.action: Maintain the function-tagged ingredient master list and promote confirmed bills into per-state rows.

us-multistate-snap-restrictions.summary: Twenty-three states approved SNAP waivers restricting sweetened or carbonated beverages, with effective dates rolling out 2026 to 2028.
us-multistate-snap-restrictions.impacts: Sweetened and possibly broadly worded zero-sugar sparkling lines may be SNAP-ineligible in some states.
us-multistate-snap-restrictions.implications: Point-of-sale eligibility now varies by state, affecting volume in SNAP-heavy channels.
us-multistate-snap-restrictions.action: Do a state-by-state read of which products are caught by the actual waiver wording.
